Whatever is it that we are all looking for? I fancy that it is really quite close. When I was a boy I had a fancy that Heaven or Fairyland or whatever I called it, was immediately behind my own back, and that this was why I could never manage to see it, however often I twisted and turned to take it by surprise. I had a notion of a man perpetually spinning round on one foot like a teetotum in the effort to find that world behind his back which continually fled from him. Perhaps this is why the world goes round. Perhaps the world is always trying to look over its shoulder and catch up the world which always escapes it, yet without which it cannot be itself.

In any case, as I have said, I think that we must always conceive of that which is the goal of all our endeavours as something which is in some strange way near. Science boasts of the distance of its stars; of the terrific remoteness of the things of which it has to speak. But poetry and religion always insist upon the proximity, the almost menacing closeness of the things with which they are concerned. Always the Kingdom of Heaven is “At Hand”; and Looking-glass Land is only through the looking-glass. So I for one should never be astonished if the next twist of a street led me to the heart of that maze in which all the mystics are lost. I should not be at all surprised if I turned one corner in Fleet Street and saw a yet queerer-looking lamp; I should not be surprised if I turned a third corner and found myself in Elfland.

I should not be surprised at this; but I was surprised the other day at something more surprising. I took a turn out of Fleet Street and found myself in England.

.....

The singular shock experienced perhaps requires explanation. In the darkest or the most inadequate moments of England there is one thing that should always be remembered about the very nature of our country. It may be shortly stated by saying that England is not such a fool as it looks. The types of England, the externals of England, always misrepresent the country. England is an oligarchical country, and it prefers that its oligarchy should be inferior to itself.

message.content:
What is it that we all seek? I believe it lies surprisingly close. As a child, I imagined that Heaven or some form of Fairyland was situated just behind me, which is why I could never catch a glimpse of it, no matter how often I turned around in an attempt to surprise it. This led me to envision a man endlessly spinning on one foot, much like a top, trying to find that elusive world that perpetually evaded him. Perhaps this is the reason the world spins. It might be that the world is eternally glancing over its shoulder, striving to reunite with what perpetually slips away, yet is essential for its very existence.

In any event, as I have mentioned, I believe that we must always envision our ultimate aspirations as being curiously close. Science boasts of the vast distances of stars and the incredible remoteness of its subjects. In contrast, poetry and religion emphasize the startling nearness and almost threatening immediacy of their matters. The Kingdom of Heaven is always described as “At Hand,” while Looking-glass Land lies just beyond the mirror. Consequently, I would not find it astonishing if a sudden turn on a street led me to the center of that intricate labyrinth where all mystics wander. It wouldn’t surprise me in the least if I turned a corner on Fleet Street and encountered an even stranger lamp; nor would I be shocked to find myself in Elfland after another turn.

While such occurrences would not baffle me, I recently found myself taken aback by something far more surprising. As I stepped off Fleet Street, I unexpectedly discovered myself in England.

The peculiar shock I felt perhaps warrants some explanation. Even during the bleakest or most challenging times, there is a fundamental truth about our nation that should never be overlooked. This can be succinctly expressed: England is not nearly as foolish as it appears. The outward representations and stereotypes associated with England often mislead those who encounter them. This country is characterized by an oligarchic structure, and it has a tendency to prefer that its oligarchy remains inferior to the populace itself.
